title: Flor and the solera
subtitle: Biological ageing and blending
objectives: Explain the classification of base wines

steps.title: Flor
steps.body: After fermentation, base wines are tasted and classified. The finest, palest are fortified to about 15 to 15.5% and put in barrels, botas, filled about five-sixths. A film of yeast, flor, grows on the surface. It protects the wine from oxygen and feeds on alcohol and glycerol, producing acetaldehyde: bready, nutty, saline aromas. This is biological ageing.

steps.title: The solera
steps.body: Sherry ages in a solera: rows of barrels of different ages. Wine is drawn from the oldest, the solera, a process called saca, never more than about a third at a time; by law, no more than 40% a year. It's replaced from the next oldest, the first criadera, and so on, a process called rocío. Young wine enters the youngest criadera. The result is a consistent blend of many ages.

steps.prompt: Put the solera's movements in order.
items: Draw from the oldest tier, the saca
Refill it from the first criadera
Refill the first criadera from the second
Add young wine to the youngest tier
steps.explanation: Wine moves step by step from young to old.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: Base wines are classified by taste. Light, delicate wines are marked for Fino and Manzanilla, fortified to 15%. Fuller wines go to Oloroso, fortified to 17%, where flor can't live. Some wines change paths during ageing, losing their flor and becoming Amontillado or Palo Cortado.

steps.prompt: At what strength can flor no longer survive?
steps.explanation: At 17%, flor dies; the wine ages with oxygen.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Flor protects Fino and adds bready, saline notes
The solera blends many ages through saca and rocío
Base wines are classified for Fino or Oloroso
